english: That actor has a small face.
tip: 얼굴이 작아요 (eolgur-i jagayo = 'the face is small') is a compliment – a small face is a Korean beauty ideal, so this is praise for the actor.

english: My friend is warm-hearted.
tip: 마음 (maeum) means heart and mind at once, so 마음이 따뜻해요 (maeum-i ttatteuthaeyo) praises someone's whole inner self as warm, not just their feelings.

english: I look like my dad.
tip: 닮았어요 (dalmasseoyo) is past tense for a present fact – Korean treats resemblance as settled long ago: you took after Dad once, and it stuck.

english: Where is that person right now?
tip: 그분 (geubun), the respectful 'that person', pulls the verb up with it: 계세요 (gyeseyo) is the honorific 'is (somewhere)', replacing plain 있어요 (isseoyo).

english: How old are you?
tip: 살 (sal) counts age with native numbers: 몇 살이에요? (myeot sar-ieyo? = how old are you?)

english: I am twenty years old.
tip: 스물 (seumul = twenty) shrinks to 스무 (seumu) before a counter: 스무 살 (seumu sal = twenty years). Korean numbers slim down to count, like 하나 (hana) becoming 한 (han).

english: Our dog is old.
tip: 나이가 많아요 (nai-ga manayo) is literally 'age is many' – Korean stacks up years instead of calling someone old, and it works for dogs too.

english: How old are you, if I may ask?
tip: 나이가 어떻게 돼요? (nai-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?) is the soft way to ask an age, roughly 'how does your age turn out?' – 몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?) is the blunt version, fine for kids.

english: Happy birthday!
tip: 축하해요 (chukahaeyo = I congratulate) attaches to any occasion word: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) is 'birthday + congratulations'. Swap in any occasion, keep the ending.

english: I'm inviting friends to the party.
tip: -들 (deul) makes plurals: 친구들 (chingu-deul = friends). Korean often skips it.

english: How do you do?
tip: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheoeum boepgetseumnida) is the set formal line for a first meeting – literally 'I meet you for the first time' – so it's never used twice with the same person.

english: This is my husband.
tip: 이쪽은 (ijjog-eun) introduces a person as 'this side is...' – pointing at a direction rather than the person is the polite Korean way to introduce someone.

english: This is my mother.
tip: 이분 (ibun), the respectful 'this person', lifts the verb ending too: 어머니세요 (eomeoni-seyo), not plain 어머니예요 (eomeoni-yeyo) – respected subjects take -세요 (-seyo).

english: Where are you from?
tip: 어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo?) is literally 'where did you come from?' – Korean asks about origin in the past tense, as a completed journey.

english: How are you doing?
tip: 잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo?) is literally 'are you getting along well?' – 지내다 (jinaeda) means to spend your days, so you're asking how life is passing.

english: Let's have coffee together tomorrow.
tip: 마셔요 (masyeoyo) can be a statement, a question, or 'let's drink' – one polite form covers all three. 같이 (gachi = together) is the clue this one is an invitation.

english: I get up at seven in the morning.
tip: 시 hours take native numbers: 일곱 시 (ilgop si = 7 o'clock).

english: I commute to work by subway.
tip: 로 (ro) marks your means of transport: 지하철로 (jihacheol-lo) = by subway. It works for any vehicle – 버스로 (beoseu-ro = by bus), 차로 (cha-ro = by car).

english: I transfer from the bus to the subway.
tip: 갈아타요 (garatayo) is built from 갈다 (galda = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – transferring between lines is literally 'change-riding'.

english: It takes forty minutes to the office.
tip: 분 minutes take Sino numbers: 사십 분 (sasip bun = 40 minutes).

english: The traffic is really bad today.
tip: 길이 막혀요 (giri makyeoyo) is literally 'the road is blocked' – Korean describes a traffic jam from the road's point of view, not the traffic's.

english: The roads are crowded at rush hour.
tip: 퇴근 시간 (toegeun sigan) = 'leaving-work time' = the evening rush hour.

english: From next week I'll bike to work.
tip: 부터 (buteo) glues straight onto a time word: 다음 주부터 (daeum ju-buteo) = starting next week. Its endpoint partner is 까지 (kkaji = until).

english: I buy coffee on the way to work.
tip: 출근길 (chulgeungil) = the way to work; -길 (gil) makes 'route' words.

english: Our company is in Seoul.
tip: 우리 회사 (uri hoesa) is 'our company' even when the listener works somewhere else – 우리 (uri) covers whatever you belong to: company, school, house.

english: Hello, Manager Kim.
tip: At work Koreans use title + 님 (nim): 과장님 (gwajangnim = manager + honorific). A colleague's bare name sounds rude – the title itself is the polite address.

english: The department head is on a business trip now.
tip: 중 (jung) after a noun means 'in the middle of it': 출장 중 (chuljang jung) = mid-business-trip. It works everywhere – 회의 중 (hoeui jung) = in a meeting.

english: The boss is in a meeting right now.
tip: -세요 adds respect for the boss: 회의 중이세요 (hoeui jungiseyo = is in a meeting).

english: The computer suddenly isn't working.
tip: 안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) is literally 'it doesn't become' – the all-purpose Korean for 'it's not working', whether it's a computer, a plan, or a request.

english: I sent the report to the department head.
tip: 께 (kke) is the honorific 'to': 부장님께 (bujangnimkke) = to the department head. With friends it's plain 한테 (hante) – same job, no deference.
